newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Belgian school shut as Zaire civil war nears Shaba.
newsitem.headline: Belgian school shut as Zaire civil war nears Shaba.

text.p: A Belgian school in Zaire's copper-mining province of Shaba closed early for Easter on Friday, as the country's former colonial masters erred on the side of caution in the face of the approaching civil war.

But as Laurent Kabila's rebels advanced towards Shaba's capital and Zaire's second city, Lubumbashi, few foreigners were expecting mayhem on the scale seen in earlier unrest in the province that has fought several times for independence.
After the psychologically crucial jungle city of Kisangani fell last weekend in the faraway north, the army in the south seems to be imploding, say politicians and business leaders.
But they believe the danger of soldiers repeating a rampage of looting which devastated the city six years ago has eased.

Expatriates seem to agree, but just in case, the Belgian school closed a week early to let families of the 1,500 foreign workers in the region leave for Easter holidays. Contingency plans for possible evacuation have also been made.
"The holidays will be three weeks instead of two and most families expect their children will be back as normal for the reopening," said Christian Merschman, the Belgian consul.
Lebanese businessmen, many of whom settled in Lubumbashi long ago, chartered a plane this week to fly their families to Johannesburg, two hours away to the south.
Other foreigners -- mainly Belgians, Greeks and Portuguese - - said they were relaxed about what all assume will be a swift and relatively bloodless transfer of power in Shaba to Kabila.
"It will all be over in a week or two and then everyone will come back," said one Indian businessman, Pralad Parkbo.
Not everyone, however, is expected to return once the rebels, presently about 400 km (250 miles) or several days away at least, enter Lubumbashi.

With Kabila rejecting a ceasefire, families of officials linked to unpopular President Mobutu Sese Seko have been leaving for the capital Kinshasa or to South Africa, expatriate sources say. The officials themselves, however, are hanging on.

"The barons of the regime have the most to fear from Kabila," said Shaba's suspended governor Kyungu wa Kumwanza, head of the province's most popular political party, UFERI -- not including himself among them.
France, despised by the rebels as Mobutu's main foreign backer, urged its nationals on Thursday to leave the vast Central African republic unless they had vital work there.
French representatives in Shaba said none of the 180 or so French expatriates, working in the mines in Lubumbashi, Kolwezi and other towns, had so far felt the need to heed the official advice.
"Hardly any of them have wives and children here and I don't know of any who have left," one said.
Kolwezi, 400 km (250 miles) northwest from Lubumbashi, is a name that still sends shudders down the spine of many Belgians.

Twenty years ago, separatist rebels massacred some of the 2,000 Belgians living in the then prosperous copper-mining town. Those rebels were seeking independence for Katanga, as Shaba is still called locally. They crossed from bases in Angola.
French paratroops took control of the town before African peacekeepers deployed and stayed for over a year.
